::: {.resource-intro}
**The essential idea:** A transparent literature search records where, when, and how you searched, as well as why sources were included or excluded. It supports defensible decisions even when the search evolves.
:::

## Core practices

### Scope the question

Identify topic, population or system, context, and type of evidence needed.

### Construct search strings

Combine synonyms with OR and different concepts with AND; check each database’s syntax.

### Log your decisions

Record search date, database, exact query, filters, results, changes, and screening reasons.

## A simple workflow

Run an initial search, record its exact settings and result count, inspect a manageable sample, then revise one search element at a time. Document the revision and why it was made.

## In context

::: {.callout-example}
For a question about eelgrass restoration and sediment, a student searches two databases, logs the two different query syntaxes, and records why studies focused only on terrestrial grasses were excluded.
:::

## Keep in mind

A documented search is not automatically a systematic review. Systematic and scoping reviews require additional design, reporting, and quality controls.
